subject: physiology
title: Hypothalamus, limbic system and thermoregulation

steps.tx: Thermoregulation depends on a **set point** in the preoptic area. When body temperature rises above this set point, heat loss mechanisms switch on, such as cutaneous vasodilatation and sweating. When it falls, heat production rises through shivering and increased voluntary activity. Radiation accounts for the largest share of heat loss at rest, followed by evaporation and conduction.
steps.say: Thermoregulation depends on a set point in the preoptic area. steps.tx: Fever raises the **set point**, so the body defends a higher temperature. Each one degree rise in body temperature increases basal metabolic rate by about 7 percent. During sleep, metabolic rate falls about 10 percent below waking levels. Rectal temperature is the best reflection of core temperature and varies least with the environment, while oral temperature runs about 0.5 degrees lower.

steps.tx: The **lateral hypothalamus** drives feeding, while the **ventromedial nucleus** provides satiety. Leptin, made by fat cells, reduces food intake by raising alpha-MSH signalling through melanocortin-4 receptors. Ghrelin, released mainly from the stomach, increases appetite and stimulates growth hormone. Orexin from the lateral hypothalamus also increases appetite. Alpha-MSH promotes satiety, while neuropeptide Y increases appetite.

steps.tx: The **suprachiasmatic nucleus** is the body's biological clock. It sits above the optic chiasm and receives light information from the retina. Light and dark cycles, called zeitgebers, keep the roughly 25 hour internal rhythm aligned to 24 hours. The pineal gland then releases melatonin at night. Destruction of the suprachiasmatic nucleus abolishes the regular sleep and wake rhythm.

steps.tx: The **limbic system** governs emotion, memory, sexual behaviour and autonomic responses. Its core structures include the cingulate gyrus, septal nuclei, hippocampus and amygdala. The Papez circuit links the hippocampus, fornix, mamillary body, anterior thalamic nucleus and cingulate gyrus. Bilateral damage to the anterior temporal lobes and amygdala causes Kluver-Bucy syndrome, with placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality, hypermetamorphosis and visual agnosia. Hyperactivity is not a feature.
